title: Benchmarking Measured Privacy Protection for LLM Adaptation
one_liner: Differential privacy offers theoretical guarantees but fails in practice when adaptation data looks like pretraining data; the real privacy risk depends on distributional distance, not just noise levels.
lead: When you fine-tune a large language model on sensitive data using differential privacy (a mathematical technique that adds noise to protect secrets), the paperwork says your data is safe. But this paper tests whether it actually is. They found something unsettling: even with the same amount of noise, a model trained on data that looks similar to its pretraining data leaks secrets badly, while models trained on completely different data stay private. The theoretical guarantee lied.

problem.h2: The privacy guarantee that does not hold in practice
paras: Large language models start their lives trained on enormous public datasets (billions of sentences from books, websites, code). Later, companies fine-tune these models on new, sensitive data—medical records, customer support conversations, proprietary code. Differential privacy is the mathematical tool used to protect these new sensitive datasets: it works by adding noise to the numbers the model adjusts during learning, creating a formal mathematical proof that no single person's data can be extracted. The proof looks airtight.

But here is the gap: the original model already learned patterns from public data. If the sensitive data you are adapting on looks similar to what the model has already seen, the model recognizes it, and sneakier attackers can still extract it even through the noise. A naive approach: just apply noise uniformly and trust the math. This breaks because what the model already learned acts like a backdoor, letting attackers reverse-engineer private sentences if they look familiar enough.

callout.b: The paper tests whether noise actually protects privacy in practice.
callout.html: They simulate attacks on fine-tuned models and measure how much of the private data can be extracted even with differential privacy, varying how similar the private data is to the original pretraining data.

panels.title: 1. The setup: a model remembers
panels.caption: Model trained on billions of public sentences. Pattern-recognition machinery now looks for familiar text.

panels.title: 2. Privacy noise applied (theory says safe)
panels.caption: Noise added during fine-tuning on sensitive data. Differential privacy math claims the data is protected.

panels.title: 3. But if new data looks like old data...
panels.caption: Attacker notices new data matches what came before. Already-learned patterns emerge easily.

panels.title: 4. Attacker can still extract it
panels.caption: Because model already knew similar text, noise fails to hide it. High leakage when data matches pretraining.

panels.title: 5. Truly different data stays hidden
panels.caption: Out-of-distribution data (completely different) actually is protected. Noise works when data is alien.

steps.text: Collect three versions of adaptation data: some directly from pretraining, some from the same distribution as pretraining, some completely different.
Adapt the pretrained model on each dataset using four different methods (full fine-tuning, LoRA, Prefix Tuning, last-layer only) with noise added.
Deploy the best-known privacy attacks (membership inference: can you tell if a specific sentence was in training; canary extraction: can you recover hidden sentences inserted into training).
Measure how many secrets the attacker extracts from each model, plotting leakage against how similar the data was to pretraining.
Compare which fine-tuning strategy (LoRA, Prefix Tuning, full, head-only) gives the best actual privacy protection for out-of-distribution data.

object.h2: The one thing the paper measures in practice
paras: Instead of trusting the mathematics, the paper measures actual privacy leakage—the number of secrets an attacker can extract from the fine-tuned model using real-world privacy attacks. This is not a theoretical proof; it is an measured test. They vary the one key thing that breaks differential privacy: how similar the adaptation data is to what the model saw during pretraining.

hidden.h2: Distributional distance: the hidden reason privacy fails
hidden.name: Distance between adaptation and pretraining data
paras: The paper introduces a hidden quantity that theory ignores: how far apart the adaptation data distribution is from the pretraining distribution, measured in a concrete way. They use sentence embeddings (converting sentences into lists of numbers that capture meaning) and compute Wasserstein distance (a mathematical measure of how different two sets of numbers are).

This hidden distance is not mentioned in the theoretical privacy proofs, yet it dominates the practical privacy risk. When distance is near zero (adaptation data looks like pretraining data), privacy leakage is high; when distance is large (adaptation data is alien), leakage drops dramatically even with the same noise level. This is the missing link between theory and practice.

heat.caption: Darker means higher privacy leakage. Overlap and IID data leak most; out-of-distribution data stays private.

reads.html: The paper measures how similar the new data is to the old data using numbers that represent sentence meaning, then compares privacy leakage across that spectrum.
They compute Sentence-BERT embeddings and Wasserstein distance between Pile pretraining subsets and each adaptation dataset.

mechanism.h2: Why the model leaks secrets when data looks familiar
paras: Here is the concrete reason: a model trained on a billion sentences has already compressed enormous amounts of knowledge about those sentences into its weights (the internal numbers). When you fine-tune on new data that looks similar, the model barely has to learn anything new—it already knows those patterns. The weight adjustments during fine-tuning are small.

Differential privacy works by saying: add noise proportional to the size of the weight change. Small changes get small noise. So when adaptation data is similar to pretraining, the changes are tiny, the noise is tiny, and an attacker who knows what the original model looked like can simply ask: what small adjustment would produce this new model? If the attacker knows the model was trained on similar data, they can reverse-engineer the private text.

In contrast, when adaptation data is completely alien (truly out-of-distribution), the model must rewrite large parts of itself to learn the new patterns. Large changes get large noise. Now an attacker cannot simply reverse the changes—the noise is too loud, drowning out any fingerprint of individual private examples. The differential privacy now does its job because what the model already learned does not interfere.

stages.s: Compute how much model weights must move
Add noise proportional to weight movement

math.words: privacy cost = (distance between weight values) / (noise clipping threshold) plus averaging over steps
symbols: the weight after fine-tuning on private data
the clipping threshold (how big a change counts as large)
the noise standard deviation (higher noise = more protection)
the privacy cost for that single weight

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Scenario A (in-distribution): Pretraining saw similar data, so weight w1 only moves 0.02 from old to new. With clipping threshold C=1.0, privacy_loss = 0.02/1.0 = 0.02. Noise needed: sigma=0.1 (weak).
Scenario B (out-of-distribution): New data is alien, weight w1 must move 0.8 to adapt. Privacy_loss = 0.8/1.0 = 0.8. Noise needed: sigma=0.8 (strong).

Same privacy budget, but in-distribution training created tiny adjustments and weak noise. Out-of-distribution training creates large adjustments and strong noise. Attacker exploits the weak-noise case more easily.

math.note: The noise is supposed to protect privacy, but only the size of the weight movement forces the noise to be large enough to matter.

charts.title: In-distribution adaptation (data similar to pretraining)
charts.note: High leakage because model already knew similar patterns. Noise level fixed by small weight changes.

charts.title: Out-of-distribution adaptation (data completely different)
charts.note: Low leakage because large weight changes force large protective noise. Same noise budget, totally different outcome.

items.html: Differential privacy offers a mathematical proof, but only in isolation. When a model carries pretraining knowledge, theory is insufficient. Measured testing is required.

An adaptation dataset might look different on the surface (medical text vs. news) but still share statistical patterns (sentence structure, vocabulary overlap) with pretraining. Wasserstein distance exposes hidden similarity.

items.b: Choosing the wrong fine-tuning method without checking data.
items.html: Full fine-tuning might seem to leak more because it touches every weight. On out-of-distribution data, full fine-tuning makes large weight movements, forcing the noise to be large. Meanwhile, LoRA on in-distribution data makes tiny weight movements (because the model already knows that data), forcing the noise to be tiny. Tiny noise is easier to attack than large noise.

items.b: Done right: measure in real tests and choose the method that fits your data.
items.html: For truly out-of-distribution private data, LoRA provides the highest measured privacy protection. For data that looks like pretraining, no method fully solves the problem, and you must collect newer pretraining data or accept lower privacy.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple experiment: pretrain a small language model on one public dataset (e.g., a subset of news articles). Then fine-tune on two adaptation datasets: one more news articles (in-distribution), one poetry (out-of-distribution). Apply the same differential privacy noise to both. Run a membership inference attack: for a sentence in the training set, can you tell if it was really used or if it is a decoy? Measure success rate for each adaptation type. Plot success rate against Wasserstein distance between adaptation and pretraining data.
demo.closing: The demo must make it impossible to miss: identical noise levels produce wildly different leakage depending on whether the private data looks like pretraining data or not. Theory alone cannot predict this gap.
